citation.title: Editorial Bias in Crowd-Sourced Political Information

standing_assumptions:
The article (PLOS ONE 10(9): e0136327, published September 2, 2015; eight pages, printed page n/8 = PDF page n) is an empirical report of randomized field experiments on Wikipedia. It has no theorem, proposition, lemma or proof, no displayed formula and no formal notation; its quantitative statements are in running text, in Fig 1 and in the tables of the twelve Supporting Information files S1–S12. The supplements are DOCX files with no fixed pagination: ‘rendered p.’ below is the page of the validators' renderings of those files, saved under the artifact folders that the targets name. Everything quoted below was read from page images: the main article from staged/pages/p-N.png, the supplements from those renderings.
(S1) Studies and populations. p. 2/8–3/8 (PDF pp. 2–3): “During the summer and fall of 2014, we conducted four studies on Wikipedia, all of which followed the same basic design. Studies 1, 2, and 4 were conducted on the English-language Wikipedia pages of the 100 current U.S. senators, while Study 3 was conducted on the 151 English-language Wikipedia pages of senators who have passed away or otherwise left the Senate since 1990 and do not currently hold any elective office or serve as a Cabinet Secretary.”
(S2) Treatments. p. 3/8 (PDF p. 3): “In each study, research assistants collected one true positive and one true negative fact from a reputable news source on each senator that was not currently mentioned on that senator’s Wikipedia page. [...] For each study, we then randomly assigned half of the pages to have a positive fact added to the page and the other half to have a negative fact added to the page.” “In Studies 1 and 4, we used a factorial design, where we also randomized half of the pages to include a citation with the fact, and the other half without a citation. In Studies 2 and 3, we always included a citation. S1–S4 Files present randomization checks and report the expected covariate balance across the treatment conditions for each study. In S5 File, we report one concluding study to replicate Studies 1 and 4 that was partially aborted due to problems in the implementation, the inclusion of which does not change the results.”
(S3) Implementation. p. 3/8 (PDF p. 3), ‘Implementation on Wikipedia’: “After the facts were collected and senators were randomly assigned to experimental conditions, we inserted the facts into the corresponding senator’s Wikipedia article in the section that seemed most appropriate. In order to prevent confounding, the order in which the edits were made, the time of day, the name of the editing Wikipedia account, and the IP address used to make the edit were randomly assigned as well. With the exception of Study 1, new accounts were created before each study began and were seeded with true, cited, political, non-Senate edits to Wikipedia. More details are presented in S1–S4 Files.” S1 File (rendered p. 1), ‘Details of Random Assignment’: “Senators were first randomly assigned into 25 blocks of 4. Within each block, 2 senators were randomly assigned to receive a negative fact and 2 were randomly assigned to receive a positive fact. Independent of the type of fact, 2 senators were randomly assigned to have the fact cited and 2 senators were randomly assigned to have the fact uncited. The date, time, and account used to make the edits were randomly assigned as well .”
(S4) Outcome and model. p. 4/8 (PDF p. 4), ‘Estimation of Experimental Effects’: “Our primary dependent variable is the survival time of the facts–the amount of time between when the fact is added to Wikipedia and when it is removed. To assess the statistical difference in the survival times between the experimental conditions, we use a Cox proportional hazard model [32].” p. 4/8, Results: “Pooling across studies, negative facts are far more likely to be removed than positive facts by other Wikipedia editors (hazard ratio = 1.59, a measure of the rate at which an event happens in one treatment group over another, p = 0.001).”
(S5) Conventions of the supplementary tables. In the Cox tables of the supplements each entry stands under ‘Coefficient:’ with a parenthesized entry under ‘Standard error:’ beneath it (S6, S9 and S10 were read for this list; finding P041-N013 records the same heading in S7 and S8), and the tables of S6, S9 and S11 used below each carry a note of the form “*Significant at the 10% level; **Significant at the 5% level; ***Significant at the 1% level; Fixed Effects refer to fixed effects for study wave; Covariates Yes means controlling for the date and time order in which an edit was randomly assigned to be made, a binary variable for Republicans, Senate class, region (NE, S, W), length of incumbency, log of Wikipedia page character count before Study 1 began, log of state population, and a dichotomous influence variable for party leaders and committee chairs.” (S10's note stops after “Fixed Effects refer to fixed effects for study wave”. The note of S6 Table E has in addition, after the legend of the stars, “^Date of entry, and hour of entry removed to avoid convergence issues;”, the caret being attached to ‘Yes^’ in the Covariates row of the column ‘5 (1st Half)’.) The entries headed ‘Coefficient:’ in the Cox tables are hazard ratios (exponentiated Cox coefficients) for positive against negative facts and for cited against uncited facts, with standard errors on the hazard-ratio scale: S6 Table A (‘Pooled Cox Regression Estimates’, rendered p. 1) prints Positive 0.629*** (0.091), N 300, and Cited 0.429*** (0.069), N 200, and the main text's 1.59 and 2.33 are their reciprocals (finding P041-N013, rated a clarity note). The paper does not say how the stars are computed.
(S6) Not in the paper: the deposited data. The replication archive (Harvard Dataverse doi:10.7910/DVN/WT4I9N, V1.0; staged/code/harvard-dataverse-WT4I9N-v1.0/) has 551 rows: 100 for each of Studies 1, 2, 4 and 5 and 151 for Study 3. Its codebook codes treatment 1 as positive and cited, 2 as positive and uncited, 3 as negative and cited, 4 as negative and uncited. Studies 1, 2 and 4 each have 50 positive and 50 negative facts; Studies 1 and 4 each have 50 cited and 50 uncited facts; Study 3 has 75 positive and 76 negative facts. Following the deposited do-file (lines 11–15), a fact counts as removed by a horizon of $h$ hours when it has a recorded removal and its stored duration in milliseconds, multiplied by $2.77778\times10^{-7}$, is at most $h$; a fact with no recorded removal survives every horizon used here. The counts used in the targets (removals by 4, 6, 12, 24, 72 and 168 hours, by study and arm) were recounted from the staged CSV when this list was fixed and agree with the validators' artifacts.
(S7) Rounding. A number printed with three decimals as $v$ stands for a value in $[v - 0.0005,\ v + 0.0005]$; a whole-number percentage $k$ is the rounding of $x$ when $k - \tfrac12 \le x < k + \tfrac12$. No quantity used below lies at a rounding tie.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: S1 File and S5 File, last sentence of ‘Description of implementation’, as repaired by Sol: random order prevents ordering by treatment and does not by itself rule out effects of earlier treatments on later edits or of the adaptive changes
canonical_claim.location: S1 File, last paragraph (rendered p. 2); S5 File, last paragraph (rendered p. 2)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Corrected text; Sol's smallest_repair, validated.json, P041-N011, verbatim] Replace the unconditional assurances in S1 and S5 with: “Random assignment of the original order prevents deliberate ordering by treatment. It does not by itself rule out treatment-dependent account responses or effects of the adaptive changes.” State which protocol and exposure conditions the causal estimand refers to if a direct-effect interpretation is retained.
[Mathematical content] Setting and notation of P041-T5: $2m$ ranks, $m$ cited (C) and $m$ uncited (U) edits, the type sequence $z$ uniformly distributed over the $\binom{2m}{m}$ balanced sequences, and $D(z)$ the cited-minus-uncited difference in mean outcomes.
(a) [What random order does give; the first sentence] Suppose the outcome of the edit at rank $r$ depends only on its rank and on its own type: $Y_r(z) = g(r, z_r)$ for a function $g : \{1, \dots, 2m\} \times \{\mathrm{C}, \mathrm{U}\} \to \mathbb{R}$, with no dependence on the types of the other edits ($g$ may vary with rank in any way, for instance because the schedule is uneven). Then $$\mathrm{E}[D] = \frac{1}{2m}\sum_{r=1}^{2m}\big(g(r,\mathrm{C}) - g(r,\mathrm{U})\big),$$ the average over ranks of the direct effect of citation. In particular, if $g(r,\mathrm{C}) = g(r,\mathrm{U}) = c_r$ for every $r$ (a fixed calendar pattern $c$ that does not depend on treatment), then $\mathrm{E}[D] = 0$; the validator's instance is $m = 2$, $c = (0,0,1,1)$.
(b) [What it does not give; the second sentence] The hypothesis of (a) cannot be dropped. In the system of P041-T5, $Y_r(z) = \mathbf{1}\{\exists\, s < r : z_s = \mathrm{U}\}$ depends on the types of earlier edits and not on $z_r$; every direct effect is 0; and $\mathrm{E}[D] = 1/(m(m+1)) \ne 0$ ($1/6$ for $m = 2$, $1/2550$ for $m = 50$), whereas under the original schedule $\mathrm{E}[D^{\mathrm{slow}}] = 0$. So a uniformly random order, with a balanced assignment independent of the order, does not imply that the expected contrast under the adaptive protocol equals the direct effect or the expected contrast under the planned protocol.
(c) [Which estimand; the last sentence of the repair] In the system of P041-T5 the three quantities that the printed sentence does not distinguish are: the average direct effect, $0$; the expected contrast under the planned (slow) protocol, $0$; the expected contrast under the implemented (accelerated) protocol, $1/(m(m+1))$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
As for P041-T5. The printed sentences being replaced are transcribed in P041-T13.
Not in the paper. The condition of (a), that an edit's outcome is a function of its own rank and its own treatment alone, is this audit's formal rendering of the assumption the repair says is missing: the absence of ‘treatment-dependent account responses’, that is, of any effect of the treatments of earlier edits on the fate of later ones. The validator states the principle in words (‘Random ordering would balance a fixed, treatment-independent calendar pattern in expectation. That correct observation does not establish the same result when earlier treatments alter the response process or the schedule’; P041-N011/v1/artifact/derivation.md, ‘Interpretation before the calculation’, emphasis marks removed) and checks the instance $m = 2$, $c = (0,0,1,1)$ exactly (exact_check.py, ‘Fixed treatment-independent calendar pattern: expected contrast = 0’). In (a) the expectation follows from $\Pr(z_r = \mathrm{C}) = \Pr(z_r = \mathrm{U}) = 1/2$ at every rank.
canonical_claim.note: The repair is a weaker conclusion, not a theorem with an added hypothesis: Sol rates its cost as weaker_conclusion and says that keeping the assurance ‘would require substantive assumptions ensuring the relevant account-history and adaptive-schedule effects cannot distort the desired contrast. Those are not minor regularity conditions and are not verified for this application.’ Part (a) in its general form is this list's statement of the sufficient condition and is not printed by the paper or written out by the validator beyond the sentence and the instance quoted in definitions_needed; a fidelity check should compare it with Sol's first sentence and with that instance, and the instance is the part to prove first. Parts (b) and (c) are corollaries of P041-T5 and should reuse its definitions. Neither part says anything about the actual study: ‘No numerical correction follows from the established defect.’ The same artifact also discusses standard errors (row-level against clustered sandwich variances); nothing there is established as an error and it is not a target.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: S11 File, Table A (‘OLS Estimates on Survival at 6 Hours and 12 Hours’), second column (6 hrs; Studies 1,4; N 200): the standard error of the Cited coefficient, printed ‘(0.645)’, corrected to (0.064)
canonical_claim.location: S11 File, Table A (rendered p. 1; the file has one page); the main article cites the table on p. 4/8 (PDF p. 4)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed; S11 Table A, second column] “Cited / Coefficient: 0.320*** / Standard error: (0.645)”; “N 200”; “Fixed Effects Yes”; “Covariates No”; “Studies 1,4”. Table note: “*Significant at the 10% level; **Significant at the 5% level; ***Significant at the 1% level; Fixed Effects refer to fixed effects for study wave”.
[Corrected; Sol's smallest_repair, validated.json, P041-E011, verbatim] “In S11 Table A, column 2, replace the Cited standard error (0.645) with (0.064). Retain the coefficient 0.320 and its three stars.”
[Mathematical content] Reading (the regression is not written out in the paper; see definitions_needed). Ordinary least squares of $y_i$ (1 if fact $i$ survives beyond 6 hours, 0 otherwise) on an intercept, $c_i$ (1 if the fact is cited) and $w_i$ (1 if the fact belongs to Study 4), over the $n = 200$ facts of Studies 1 and 4, with the heteroskedasticity-robust covariance $$\widehat V = \frac{n}{n-k}\,(X^\top X)^{-1}\Big(\sum_i e_i^2\,x_i x_i^\top\Big)(X^\top X)^{-1},\qquad k = 3,\quad x_i = (1, c_i, w_i)^\top,\quad e_i = y_i - x_i^\top\hat\beta.$$ Data: each of the four (study, cited) cells has 50 facts, and the numbers surviving beyond 6 hours are 12 (Study 1, uncited), 25 (Study 1, cited), 23 (Study 4, uncited) and 42 (Study 4, cited).
(i) [The printed cell contradicts its own stars] $0.320/0.645 = 64/129 < 1$. A coefficient less than one standard error from zero is not significant at the 10% level, and so not at the 1% level that ‘***’ asserts (its two-sided p value is about 0.62).
(ii) [The fit] $X^\top X = \begin{pmatrix}200&100&100\\100&100&50\\100&50&100\end{pmatrix}$, $X^\top y = (102,\ 67,\ 65)^\top$, $(X^\top X)^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}3/200&-1/100&-1/100\\-1/100&1/50&0\\-1/100&0&1/50\end{pmatrix}$ and $\hat\beta = (21/100,\ 8/25,\ 7/25)^\top$. The Cited coefficient is $8/25 = 0.320$, as printed; it equals $\tfrac12\big(\tfrac{25-12}{50} + \tfrac{42-23}{50}\big)$.
(iii) [The robust variance] The fitted values in the four cells, in the order above, are $21/100$, $53/100$, $49/100$ and $81/100$, and the sums of squared residuals in the four cells are $1833/200$, $2509/200$, $2493/200$ and $1353/200$, so $\sum_i e_i^2 = 2047/50$. The Cited row of $(X^\top X)^{-1}$ applied to $x_i$ is $-1/100$ for an uncited and $+1/100$ for a cited fact, with square $1/10000$ for every $i$. Hence $$\widehat V_{cc} = \frac{200}{197}\cdot\frac{1}{10000}\cdot\frac{2047}{50} = \frac{2047}{492500}.$$
(iv) [The corrected cell] $0.0635^2 \le \tfrac{2047}{492500} < 0.0645^2$, so the standard error $\sqrt{2047/492500} = 0.06446\ldots$ rounds to $0.064$; it is not the printed $0.645$ ($0.645^2 = 16641/40000 \ne 2047/492500$).
(v) [The stars are right with the corrected value] $t^2 = (8/25)^2\big/\tfrac{2047}{492500} = \tfrac{50432}{2047} > 24 > 2.61^2$, so $|t| > 4.89$, beyond the two-sided 1% critical value of the $t$ distribution with 197 degrees of freedom (about 2.601) and of the standard normal (about 2.576).

canonical_claim.note: A misplaced decimal in one cell of a supplementary table, rated Minor; it is a target because the author's instruction covers every confirmed error at any severity and because both the refutation and the correction are exact: part (i) uses only the printed cell and its legend, and parts (ii) to (v) are rational arithmetic from four counts. The validator's script (P041-E011/v1/artifact/check.py, results.json) carries out (ii) and (iii) in exact rationals and checks the bracketing in (iv); the same script reproduces the other three Cited standard errors of S11 (0.0646, 0.0624, 0.0533 against the printed 0.065, 0.062, 0.053). The unrounded standard error is 0.06447, so the corrected three-decimal entry is 0.064 and not 0.065. The p values quoted in words (0.62 at the printed cell, about 1.5e-6 at the corrected one) involve the $t$ distribution and are not part of the target; (i) and (v) are stated as comparisons of $|t|$ with 1 and with 2.61. The general fact behind the Cited coefficient in (ii), that with treatment balanced within each study the coefficient is the mean of the within-study differences, is used again in P041-T9.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The significance markers of four cells of the Cox tables: S6 Table B, Positive (‘0.670**’); S6 Table E, Cited, Study 5 (1st Half) (‘0.480*’) and Positive, Study 5 (2nd Half) (‘0.274*’); S9 Table A, Positive X NE Region, first column (‘0.316***’); corrected to ***, **, ** and **
canonical_claim.location: S6 File, Table B (rendered p. 2) and Table E (rendered p. 3); S9 File, Table A (rendered p. 1); the main article cites S6 and S9 on p. 4/8 (PDF p. 4)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] S6 Table B (‘Covariate Adjusted Cox Regression Pooled Estimates’), first column: “Positive / Coefficient: 0.670** / Standard error: (0.095)”; N 300; Fixed Effects Yes; Covariates Yes; Studies 1,2,4. S6 Table E (‘Study by Study Cox Regression Estimates, with Covariate Adjustment’), column ‘5 (1st Half)’: “Cited / Coefficient: 0.480* / Standard error: (0.174)”, N 50, Covariates ‘Yes^’ (note: “^Date of entry, and hour of entry removed to avoid convergence issues”); column ‘5 (2nd Half)’: “Positive / Coefficient: 0.274* / Standard error: (0.162)”, N 50. S9 Table A (‘Covariates as Moderators of Positive Edits from Cox Regressions’), first column: “Positive X NE Region / Coefficient: 0.316*** / Standard error: (0.149)”; N 300; Studies 1,2,4. Legend of each table: “*Significant at the 10% level; **Significant at the 5% level; ***Significant at the 1% level”.
[Corrected; Sol's smallest_repair, validated.json, P041-E012, verbatim] “Change S6 Table B Positive 0.670** to 0.670***; S6 Table E Study 5 first-half Cited 0.480* to 0.480**; S6 Table E Study 5 second-half Positive 0.274* to 0.274**; and S9 Table A first-column Positive X NE Region 0.316*** to 0.316**.”
[Mathematical content] Reading (the paper does not say how the stars are computed; see definitions_needed). A cell prints a hazard ratio $h \in (0,1)$ and its delta-method standard error $s > 0$ on the hazard-ratio scale; the Wald statistic of the log hazard ratio is $z(h,s) = \log(h)\big/(s/h) = h\log(h)/s$; the two-sided normal p value is $p(h,s) = 2\,\Phi(-|z(h,s)|)$; and a cell carries ‘***’ when $p < 0.01$, ‘**’ when $0.01 \le p < 0.05$, ‘*’ when $0.05 \le p < 0.10$ and no star otherwise. Equivalently, with $c_{.01} = 2.5758\ldots$, $c_{.05} = 1.9599\ldots$ and $c_{.10} = 1.6448\ldots$ the points at which $2\,\Phi(-c_\alpha) = \alpha$: ‘***’ if and only if $|z| > c_{.01}$; ‘**’ if and only if $c_{.05} < |z| \le c_{.01}$; ‘*’ if and only if $c_{.10} < |z| \le c_{.05}$. Each printed number $v$ stands for a value in $[v - 0.0005,\ v + 0.0005]$.
For every $(h, s)$ in the rounding rectangle of the printed pair:
(i) S6 Table B, Positive, $(0.670,\ 0.095)$: $|z| > 2.80 > c_{.01}$, so $p < 0.01$. (At the printed pair $z = -2.82442\ldots$ and $p = 0.0047366\ldots$; over the rectangle $0.0044 < p < 0.0051$.) The tier is ‘***’, not the printed ‘**’.
(ii) S6 Table E, Cited, Study 5 (1st Half), $(0.480,\ 0.174)$: $c_{.05} < 2.01 < |z| < 2.04 < c_{.01}$, so $0.01 < p < 0.05$. ($z = -2.02474\ldots$, $p = 0.0428938\ldots$; $0.041 < p < 0.045$.) The tier is ‘**’, not the printed ‘*’.
(iii) S6 Table E, Positive, Study 5 (2nd Half), $(0.274,\ 0.162)$: $c_{.05} < 2.18 < |z| < 2.20 < c_{.01}$, so $0.01 < p < 0.05$. ($z = -2.18967\ldots$, $p = 0.0285475\ldots$; $0.027 < p < 0.030$.) The tier is ‘**’, not the printed ‘*’.
(iv) S9 Table A, Positive X NE Region, first column, $(0.316,\ 0.149)$: $c_{.05} < 2.43 < |z| < 2.46 < c_{.01}$, so $0.01 < p < 0.05$. ($z = -2.44319\ldots$, $p = 0.0145578\ldots$; $0.0139 < p < 0.0152$.) The tier is ‘**’, not the printed ‘***’.
(v) [Which printed markers are false under which reading] In (i) to (iii) the printed marker names a weaker level than the one attained (significance at 1% implies significance at 5%, and at 5% implies at 10%), so if the legend is read as nested cut-offs only the marker of (iv) asserts something false: significance at the 1% level, where $p > 0.0139$. Under the usual reading, in which a cell carries the marker of the strongest level it attains, all four printed markers are wrong.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed:
From the paper. The four cells and the legend, as transcribed in the statement; the table conventions: standing assumption (S5). In S9 Table A the entry is an exponentiated interaction coefficient, a ratio of hazard ratios with null value 1; the calculation is the same. The neighbouring cells, for comparison of tiers: S6 Table B, Cited 0.352*** (0.055), N 200; S6 Table E, Study 5 (1st Half), Positive 0.387*** (0.139); S9 Table A, second column (N 400, Studies 1,2,4,5), Positive X NE Region 0.472* (0.192).
Not in the paper. (a) The reading of the stars (validator, P041-E012/v1/artifact/derivation.md, ‘Reading the numbers and the stars’ and ‘Wald calculation step by step’): the deposited do-file fits these models with ‘stcox …, robust’, whose displayed estimates are exponentiated coefficients with standard errors $s = h\sqrt{V}$, where $V$ is the robust variance of the log hazard ratio $\beta$; the test of $\beta = 0$ is $z = \beta/\sqrt{V} = h\log(h)/s$ with a normal reference. The validator's refits reproduce the four printed pairs to three decimals and give the same four tiers (p = 0.00455, 0.04343, 0.02851, 0.01444). (b) The critical values: $c_{.01} = 2.5758293\ldots$, $c_{.05} = 1.9599640\ldots$, $c_{.10} = 1.6448536\ldots$. (c) The validator's certified enclosures of $p$ over the four rounding rectangles (rounded outwards; exact rational bounds on $\log$, on $\int_0^z e^{-t^2/2}\,dt$ and on $\sqrt{2/\pi}$): $[0.004416378,\ 0.005073862]$, $[0.041792640,\ 0.044011941]$, $[0.027554610,\ 0.029563591]$, $[0.013945057,\ 0.015189259]$ (P041-E012/v1/artifact/checks.txt, check_markers.py). (d) The ranges of $|z|$ over the rectangles, computed when this list was fixed: $[2.8064,\ 2.8426]$, $[2.0181,\ 2.0314]$, $[2.1820,\ 2.1974]$, $[2.4345,\ 2.4520]$.
canonical_claim.note: Four significance markers one tier off, rated Minor. It is a target because the author's instruction covers every confirmed error at any severity and because the error is decided by the printed numbers alone: the estimate and standard error beside each marker determine its tier whatever values the rounding conceals. The refutation of the printed markers and the corrected markers are the same computation, so one target carries both; the validator's evidence type is exact_counterexample. The comparisons of $|z|$ with the critical values need rational enclosures of a logarithm (for the bounds on $|z|$) and of the normal critical values (or of the normal integral); the validator's certificate shows one way to obtain them without floating point. The statements in terms of $|z|$ and the fixed numbers 2.80, 2.01, 2.04, 2.18, 2.20, 2.43, 2.46 are the parts to prove; the p values in parentheses are for the reader. $h\,|\log h|$ decreases in $h$ on the first two rectangles ($h > 1/e$) and increases on the last two (0.274 and 0.316 lie below $1/e$), so either bound the two factors separately, as the validator does, or use the monotonicity on each side. No estimate, standard error or joint test changes; the Northeast interaction remains significant at 5%.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: S11 File, opening paragraph, second sentence (‘These results, presented in Tables A and B estimate the likelihood that an edit was removed by that point in time’), corrected: the outcome of Tables A and B is survival beyond the horizon, and the printed coefficients are the negatives of the removal coefficients
canonical_claim.location: S11 File, first paragraph and Tables A and B (rendered p. 1); the main article cites the tables on p. 4/8 (PDF p. 4)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed; S11, first paragraph] “As a final robustness check, we examined the ordinary least squares estimates on survival at 6, 12, and 24 hours as well as 7 days. These results, presented in Tables A and B estimate the likelihood that an edit was removed by that point in time. The OLS estimates consistently find that for active senators, positive and cited facts are less likely to have been removed while for retired and dead senators (Study 3) there is no difference.” Table titles: “Table A: OLS Estimates on Survival at 6 Hours and 12 Hours”; “Table B: OLS Estimates on Survival at 24 Hours and 7 Days”. Printed coefficients, in the order Positive (N 300, Studies 1,2,4) | Cited (N 200, Studies 1,4) | Positive (N 151, Studies 3): 6 hrs: 0.113** | 0.320*** | -0.027; 12 hrs: 0.153*** | 0.370*** | -0.027; 24 hrs: 0.147*** | 0.390*** | -0.027; 7 Days: 0.127*** | 0.230*** | -0.054.
[Corrected; Sol's smallest_repair, validated.json, P041-E010, verbatim] “Replace was removed by that point in time with survived beyond that point in time in S11's second sentence. The corrected sentence is: These results, presented in Tables A and B, estimate the likelihood that an edit survived beyond that point in time. To reproduce the printed tables with the staged Yale do-file, also initialize each of hour6, hour12, hour24, and day7 to 1 and set it to 0 when hours_alive is at or below its horizon, matching Harvard lines 147–154.”
[Mathematical content] For a horizon of $h$ hours let $S_i(h) = 1$ if fact $i$ is not removed within $h$ hours and $0$ otherwise, and $R_i(h) = 1 - S_i(h)$.
(i) [Complementing the outcome reverses every slope] Let $X$ be an $n \times k$ real matrix of full column rank whose first column is the vector of ones $\mathbf{1}$, let $S \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $R = \mathbf{1} - S$. Then the least-squares coefficient vectors satisfy $\hat\beta_R = e_1 - \hat\beta_S$ with $e_1 = (1, 0, \dots, 0)^\top$: the intercept becomes one minus the intercept and every other coefficient changes sign. The residuals satisfy $u_R = -u_S$, so $\sum_i u_i^2\,x_i x_i^\top$, the robust covariance $\frac{n}{n-k}(X^\top X)^{-1}\big(\sum_i u_i^2\,x_i x_i^\top\big)(X^\top X)^{-1}$ and the standard errors are the same for the two outcomes.
(ii) [The printed coefficients are survival slopes] Models: (P) $S(h)$ on an intercept, the indicator of a positive fact and the indicators of Study 2 and of Study 4, over the 300 facts of Studies 1, 2, 4 (50 positive and 50 negative in each study); (C) $S(h)$ on an intercept, the indicator of a cited fact and the indicator of Study 4, over the 200 facts of Studies 1 and 4 (50 cited and 50 uncited in each); (F) $S(h)$ on an intercept and the indicator of a positive fact, over the 151 facts of Study 3 (75 positive, 76 negative). In (P) and (C) the treatment is balanced within every study, so the treatment coefficient is the difference between the two arms in the pooled proportion surviving; in (F) it is the difference in proportions. Numbers surviving beyond $h$ (treated arm, comparison arm): (P), of 150 and 150: $h = 6$: 105, 88; $h = 12$: 98, 75; $h = 24$: 90, 68; $h = 168$: 68, 49. (C), of 100 and 100: $h = 6$: 67, 35; $h = 12$: 63, 26; $h = 24$: 58, 19; $h = 168$: 34, 11. (F), of 75 and 76: $h = 6, 12, 24$: 72, 75; $h = 168$: 68, 73. The treatment coefficients are therefore (P) $17/150$, $23/150$, $11/75$, $19/150$; (C) $8/25$, $37/100$, $39/100$, $23/100$; (F) $-51/1900$, $-51/1900$, $-51/1900$, $-307/5700$. Each is within $0.0005$ of the printed entry: $0.113$, $0.153$, $0.147$, $0.127$; $0.320$, $0.370$, $0.390$, $0.230$; $-0.027$, $-0.027$, $-0.027$, $-0.054$.
(iii) [They are not removal slopes] By (i), with the outcome ‘removed by that point in time’, $R(h)$, the same twelve regressions give the negatives of these twelve numbers, for example $-17/150$ (which rounds to $-0.113$) for positive facts at 6 hours. Each printed coefficient is non-zero and has the sign of the survival slope, so none of the twelve is the rounding of the removal slope. Read as effects on removal, the printed positive coefficients for active senators would also contradict the paragraph's third sentence (‘positive and cited facts are less likely to have been removed’).

canonical_claim.statement:
[Printed] S9 Table A (‘Covariates as Moderators of Positive Edits from Cox Regressions’): “Positive X Length of Incumbency / Coefficient: 0.989 | 0.981 / Standard error: (0.019) | (0.017)” (columns: N 300, Studies 1,2,4 | N 400, Studies 1,2,4,5). S9 Table B (‘Covariates as Moderators of Cited Edits from Cox Regressions’): “Cited X Length of Incumbency / Coefficient: 1.056*** | 1.056*** / Standard error: (0.020) | (0.019)”. S10 (‘Covariates Predicting Length of Survival from Cox Regressions’): “Incumbency Length / Coefficient: 1.004 / Standard error: (0.008)” (N 400, Studies 1,2,4,5). Deposited codebook, p. 1: “lengthofincumbency: Year Senator was first elected.”
[Corrected; Sol's smallest_repair, validated.json, P041-E004, verbatim] “Relabel the S9 rows Positive X First-election year and Cited X First-election year and the S10 row First-election year; correct accompanying lists describing this same fitted covariate. Optionally specify that larger years indicate shorter tenure. If retaining tenure labels, use L=2014-Y and transform the year main effect, interactions, associated treatment main effects, baseline, and covariance matrix as derived in artifact/derivation.md.”
[Mathematical content] Let $Y$ be the year of first election (the fitted covariate), $C = 2014$, $L = C - Y$ the length of tenure in years, $T \in \{0,1\}$ a treatment indicator (positive, or cited) and $w$ the remainder of the linear predictor. The fitted Cox hazard is $h(t \mid T, Y, w) = h_0(t)\exp(bY + aT + gTY + w)$.
(i) [Reparameterization] For all real $a, b, g, C, L, T, w$: $b(C - L) + aT + gT(C - L) + w = Cb + (-b)L + (a + Cg)T + (-g)TL + w$. Hence, with $b_L = -b$, $a_L = a + Cg$, $g_L = -g$ and $h_{0,L}(t) = h_0(t)\,e^{Cb}$, $$h_{0,L}(t)\exp(b_L L + a_L T + g_L TL + w) = h_0(t)\exp(bY + aT + gTY + w)\quad\text{whenever } Y = C - L:$$ the same fitted hazards, written in terms of tenure.
(ii) [Direction] The treatment hazard ratio at tenure $L$ is $\exp(a_L + g_L L)$, and one more year of tenure multiplies it by $e^{g_L} = e^{-g} = 1/e^{g}$, the reciprocal of the printed interaction ratio $r = e^{g}$. In S10's model (no terms in $T$) one more year of tenure multiplies the hazard by $e^{-b} = 1/e^{b}$. So a printed ratio below 1 corresponds to a ratio per year of tenure above 1, and conversely: the printed S9 Table A entries ($0.989$, $0.981$) correspond to tenure ratios above 1, and the printed S9 Table B entries ($1.056$, $1.056$) and S10 entry ($1.004$) to tenure ratios below 1. Read under their printed labels, as ratios per year of incumbency, all five entries have the direction reversed.
(iii) [Magnitudes from the printed entries] For every $r$ in the rounding interval $[v - 0.0005,\ v + 0.0005]$ of a printed $v$: for $v = 0.989$, $1.0106 < 1/r < 1.0117$; for $v = 0.981$, $1.0188 < 1/r < 1.0199$; for $v = 1.056$, $0.9465 < 1/r < 0.9475$, so that $1/r$ rounds to $0.947$; for $v = 1.004$, $0.9955 < 1/r < 0.9966$.
(iv) [Standard errors and tests] If $s = r\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(g)}$ is the delta-method standard error of $r = e^{g}$, the delta-method standard error of $1/r = e^{-g}$ is $(1/r)\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(g)} = s/r^2$, and the Wald statistic for no moderation is unchanged, $(-g)^2/\operatorname{Var}(g) = g^2/\operatorname{Var}(g)$. The three stars of the S9 Table B row therefore stand, with the direction reversed.
(v) [The validator's exact instance] Take $r = 132/125 = 1.056$ and relative hazards $r^{\,T(Y - 2009)}$. At $Y = 2009$ ($L = 5$) the treatment hazard ratio is $1$; at $Y = 2008$ ($L = 6$) it is $125/132 < 1$. One more year of first election multiplies the treatment hazard ratio by $132/125 > 1$, one more year of tenure multiplies it by $125/132 < 1$, and the product of the two multipliers is 1.
